lead: Scaling builds the same circuit with smaller devices. Shrink the channel length, the oxide thickness and the supply voltage together by a factor S and the electric field inside the transistor does not change, so the device still works. Shrink only the lengths and the gate slowly loses control of the channel. Below about a quarter micrometre that loss shows up as a family of short-channel effects: threshold roll-off, drain-induced barrier lowering, punch-through, hot carriers and slow reliability drift. Every node you name — 28 nm, 7 nm — is described by these numbers.
prereq: You need: 1.3 for the drain current equations and 1.4 for velocity saturation and channel length modulation.

sections.h3: Constant-field scaling by a factor S

blocks.text: Pick a factor S > 1. Divide the channel length L, the width W, the oxide thickness t<sub>ox</sub> and every voltage (V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>T</sub>) by S. Multiply the channel doping N<sub>A</sub> by S.

Why together? Field is voltage divided by distance. Both fall by S, so the field pattern inside the device is unchanged. Some syllabi call this constant-field scaling, or Dennard scaling after the 1974 paper that proposed it.

Now follow the consequences. Oxide capacitance per unit area is C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub>, so C<sub>ox</sub> multiplies by S. The parameter κ = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>(W/L) also multiplies by S, because W/L is a ratio and does not change.

items: Drain current I<sub>D</sub> ∝ κ(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)² → S × (1/S)² = 1/S.
Delay τ = CV<sub>DD</sub>/I<sub>D</sub> → (1/S)(1/S)/(1/S) = 1/S, so the clock can rise by S.
Area per gate = WL → 1/S², so power per gate divided by area stays at 1.

blocks.where: P is the dynamic power of one gate in watts, C is its capacitance in farads, V<sub>DD</sub> is the supply in volts and f is the clock frequency in hertz. Here f scales as S because delay scales as 1/S.

blocks.text: That last line is the prize: the same watts per square millimetre, S² times more gates on the chip.

sections.h3: Constant-voltage scaling and the power wall

blocks.text: Hold V<sub>DD</sub> fixed instead and let only the lengths shrink. Field now rises by S, carriers hit velocity saturation, and the current grows only as S. Delay = CV/I<sub>D</sub> → (1/S)(1)/(S) = 1/S². Power per gate = C·V<sub>DD</sub>²·f → (1/S)(1)(S²) = S, so each gate burns S times more, not less.

Power density = S ÷ (1/S²) = S³. With S = 2 that is eight times the heat per square millimetre for the same circuit. This is why V<sub>DD</sub> fell from 5 V in the early 1990s to about 1 V, and why the fall stopped around 2005.
Once V<sub>DD</sub> was pinned near a volt, constant-field scaling ended. Clock frequency stalled at a few gigahertz and processors went multicore instead of faster.

sections.h3: Short-channel effects: roll-off, DIBL, punch-through, tunnelling

blocks.text: Below L ≈ 0.25 µm the drain is close enough that its field reaches the source end of the channel. The gate no longer owns the channel charge alone.

items: Threshold roll-off: the depletion charge under the gate is shared with the source and drain junctions. The gate has less bulk charge to support before inversion, so V<sub>T</sub> falls as L falls. A V<sub>T</sub> versus L plot drops sharply at short L.

DIBL (drain-induced barrier lowering): raising V<sub>DS</sub> lowers the potential barrier at the source end, so V<sub>T</sub> falls as V<sub>DS</sub> rises. A DIBL of 100 mV/V means V<sub>T</sub> is 100 mV lower at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.1 V than at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.1 V. The output curve gains slope in saturation, like channel length modulation but from a different cause, and off-state leakage rises.

Punch-through: at high V<sub>DS</sub> the drain and source depletion regions meet below the channel. The gate loses control completely and a large current flows whatever V<sub>GS</sub> is. Fixes are heavier doping, halo (pocket) implants near source and drain, and a thinner oxide.

GIDL (gate-induced drain leakage): in the off state (V<sub>GS</sub> = 0 or negative for nMOS) the bands bend sharply in the gate-drain overlap and electrons tunnel out of the valence band, adding drain leakage.
Gate tunnel current: below tox ≈ 2 nm electrons tunnel straight through the oxide. It grows exponentially as the oxide thins, and it is one reason oxide scaling stopped. See 1.7.

sections.h3: Hot carriers, LDD, NBTI and oxide breakdown

blocks.text: Hot carriers: the lateral field peaks near the drain. Electrons there gain enough energy to cross into the oxide or to break Si-H bonds at the interface, creating traps. V<sub>T</sub> shifts and g<sub>m</sub> falls over months of use. A lightly doped drain (LDD) places an n⁻ region between channel and n⁺ drain, so the voltage drops over a longer distance and the peak field falls. The cost is extra series resistance and less drive current.

NBTI (negative bias temperature instability): a pMOS held at a negative gate voltage and high temperature slowly builds interface traps. Its |V<sub>T</sub>| rises by tens of millivolts over years, so the gate gets slower. It partly recovers when the stress is removed. The nMOS counterpart is PBTI.

TDDB (time-dependent dielectric breakdown): a thin oxide carries stress until a percolation path forms and it shorts. It is random, so it sets a lifetime specification rather than a design rule. Taken together, these effects are why the planar transistor ran out of gate control below about 28 nm, and why the gate moved onto a fin in 1.8.

figure.caption: Read each row as the factor by which that quantity changes when the process is scaled by S. Power per gate falls fastest, so power density stays at 1.

spec.title: Constant-field scaling by factor S
spec.aria: A scaling table: lengths and supply voltage divide by S, doping multiplies by S, capacitance, current and delay divide by S, and power per gate falls as 1 over S squared, so power density is unchanged.

examples.question: A gate in a 0.25 µm process drives a load of C = 10 fF at V<sub>DD</sub> = 2.5 V with a 100 MHz clock. The process is scaled to 0.125 µm using constant-field rules. Find the dynamic power before and after scaling, and the ratio between them.
steps: Before scaling: P = C·V<sub>DD</sub>²·f = (10 × 10⁻¹⁵ F)(2.5 V)²(100 × 10⁶ Hz) = 10⁻¹⁴ × 6.25 × 10⁸ = 6.25 × 10⁻⁶ W.
New capacitance C′ = C/S = 10 fF ÷ 2 = 5 fF.
New supply V<sub>DD</sub>′ = V<sub>DD</sub>/S = 2.5 V ÷ 2 = 1.25 V.
Delay halves, so the clock doubles: f′ = 200 MHz.
Ratio P/P′ = 6.25 ÷ 1.5625 = 4 = S². Area also fell by 4, so power per unit area is unchanged.
examples.answer: 6.25 µW before scaling and 1.5625 µW after; power per gate falls by S² = 4 and power density stays the same.
examples.check:
C = 10e-15
V = 2.5
f = 100e6
P1 = C * V**2 * f
print(round(P1 * 1e6, 6))
S = 2
C2 = C / S
V2 = V / S
f2 = f * S
P2 = C2 * V2**2 * f2
print(round(P2 * 1e6, 6))
print(round(P1 / P2, 6))

traps: Power density: only constant-field scaling keeps it at 1. If V<sub>DD</sub> is held fixed you get S³, not S or S². This is the examiner's favourite version of the question.
Delay: constant-field delay scales as 1/S. The 1/S² answer belongs to constant-voltage scaling. Reading off the wrong table costs the whole mark.

DIBL versus punch-through: DIBL is a drain-field shift of V<sub>T</sub> while the gate still controls the channel; punch-through is the source and drain depletion regions meeting, after which the gate controls nothing.
Roll-off direction: VT falls as L falls. The body effect in 1.2 raises VT when VSB rises — a different knob, easy to mix up.
NBTI shifts the pMOS threshold under negative gate bias at temperature; PBTI is the nMOS counterpart. Also do not quote a fixed millivolt number — the shift depends on stress time and temperature.

quiz.q: State the constant-field scaling rules for L, t<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>DD</sub>, V<sub>T</sub> and N<sub>A</sub> when the scale factor is S.
quiz.a: L, t<sub>ox</sub>, V<sub>DD</sub> and V<sub>T</sub> divide by S; N<sub>A</sub> multiplies by S.

quiz.q: Define DIBL and give its unit.
quiz.a: Drain-induced barrier lowering: the drain voltage lowers the source-end barrier so V<sub>T</sub> falls as V<sub>DS</sub> rises. It is quoted in mV/V.

quiz.q: Why does constant-field scaling keep power density constant while constant-voltage scaling does not?
quiz.a: Constant field: power per gate ∝ 1/S² and area ∝ 1/S², so the ratio is 1. Constant voltage: power per gate ∝ S while area still ∝ 1/S², so the ratio is S³.

quiz.q: A gate has C = 20 fF, V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V and f = 200 MHz. Scale by S = 3 with constant-field rules and find the new dynamic power.
A device shows V<sub>T</sub> = 0.30 V at V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.1 V and V<sub>T</sub> = 0.20 V at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.1 V. Find the DIBL in mV/V.
quiz.a: ΔV<sub>T</sub> = 0.30 − 0.20 = 0.10 V = 100 mV over ΔV<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V, so DIBL = 100 mV/V.

quiz.q: Distinguish GIDL from gate tunnel current.
quiz.a: GIDL is band-to-band tunnelling in the gate-drain overlap in the off state and appears as drain leakage. Gate tunnel current is electrons tunnelling straight through a thin oxide from gate to channel, so it is gate leakage.

quiz.q: An LDD structure lowers the peak field near the drain. What does it cost, and why is the trade usually accepted?
quiz.a: The n⁻ region adds series resistance, so drive current and g<sub>m</sub> fall and the gate is slower. The trade is accepted because hot-carrier degradation would otherwise shift V<sub>T</sub> and shorten the chip lifetime; reliability margins cost more than a small loss of speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Constant-field scaling is history now: the supply stopped falling around 2005, so the roadmap moved to strained silicon, high-k metal gate stacks, FinFETs and now gate-all-around nanosheet transistors with backside power delivery. The effects in this chapter are the working vocabulary of the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems, which publishes projected L, t<sub>ox</sub> and V<sub>DD</sub> for each node. DIBL and NBTI extraction are still active reliability-physics problems. Search for "Dennard scaling", "DIBL extraction" and "IRDS roadmap" to go further.
